title: User Stories + Acceptance Criteria
description: User stories that the team can actually build against — versus the As-a/I-want/So-that template that contains no information. The story is the title; the AC is the contract. The discipline is that the AC is testable, observable, and specific enough to settle disputes without further conversation.

worked_examples.title: Customer-portal — Admin: role-assignment changes (CP-201)
worked_examples.content_md:
# Story: Admin can change a user's role from admin to viewer
_ID: CP-201 · size: 3 points · owner: [PO] · status: ready_

## The narrative

**As a** customer admin on the new portal,
**I want** to change another user's role from 'admin' to 'viewer' (or vice versa)
**so that** I can manage permissions without raising a ticket to our internal CS team.

## Context

Currently top-12 customers raise an average of 4 role-change tickets per week to our CS team. Each ticket takes ~12 minutes of CS time. This story lands the most common variant (admin↔viewer) and unlocks the CS-time recovery committed to in the programme business case. The 'add additional roles beyond admin/viewer' is explicitly out of scope and a Phase-2 candidate.

## Acceptance criteria

1. **Given** a customer admin viewing the user list, **when** they click the role dropdown next to another user, **then** they can select 'admin' or 'viewer' and the change is saved within 2 seconds.
2. **Given** a customer admin changes another user's role, **when** the change saves, **then** an entry is written to the audit log (CP-145) recording the actor, target, old role, new role, and timestamp.
3. **Given** a customer admin attempts to change their OWN role to 'viewer', **when** they confirm, **then** the system blocks the change with an error: 'You can't change your own admin role. Ask another admin in your organisation.'
4. **Given** an organisation has only one admin (the actor), **when** they attempt to change that role to 'viewer', **then** the system blocks with: 'There must be at least one admin in your organisation.'
5. **Given** the role change succeeds, **when** the affected user next logs in, **then** they see their new permission level reflected immediately.

## Out of scope

- Custom roles beyond 'admin' / 'viewer' (Phase 2; tracked as CP-401).
- Bulk role-assignment for multiple users at once (separate story CP-217).
- Role-change notifications via email to the affected user (separate story; AC 5 covers the in-portal reflection).

## Open questions

- None. Resolved at refinement on 24 April.

annotations.note: Title verb-led, 6-10 words. 'Admin can change a user's role' tells you the actor and the action immediately. 'Role-assignment changes' (which is what the backlog item was called) is fine for a backlog title but doesn't work as a story title.
Specific user type. 'Customer admin on the new portal' — not just 'user'. The 'As a user' story is the most common rookie mistake; it tells the developer nothing about the actor's actual context.

Context paragraph is optional but high-value. It tells the team WHY the story is being built — and the team that knows why builds better stories. Without it, the developer makes assumptions about edge-case handling that may not match the actual user.

AC in Given/When/Then form is the contract. Each one testable. The 'Given an organisation has only one admin…' criterion (AC 4) is the kind of edge case that a sloppy AC misses and a real customer hits in week one.
Out-of-scope section saves you the PR-review argument. Without it, a developer might 'helpfully' add bulk role-assignment because they thought it was the natural extension. With it, they don't.

common_mistakes: 'As a user' instead of a specific user type. 'User' is everybody and nobody; the actor matters.
AC that aren't testable. 'The system should be intuitive' isn't AC; it's a wish. 'When the admin clicks the dropdown, the change saves within 2 seconds' is AC.
AC that describe implementation. 'Use OAuth for authentication' is a solution, not a capability. 'The user authenticates without remembering a separate password' is the AC.
Out-of-scope section omitted because 'obvious'. The PR review will surface the 'but we should also…' conversation; save the time and write it down.
Open-questions section omitted because there are no open questions (you say). There always are; the discipline forces you to find them.
Stories with no number on them. 1, 2, 3 in the AC list — without numbers, refinement conversations devolve into 'the third bullet' / 'no the fourth one' / 'wait, you mean the one about admins?'.
variant_patterns: Discovery / spike story variant: no AC in the traditional sense. The AC becomes 'we have a defensible decision document with options A/B/C and a recommendation' — the deliverable is a decision, not working software.
Bug-fix story variant: 'The narrative' becomes 'expected behaviour / actual behaviour / impact'. AC becomes 'reproduce the bug, fix it, add a regression test, deploy'.

Cross-team story variant: add a §5 'Dependency contract' — what we agreed with the other team to deliver, when, and what we're delivering back to them. Misalignment here is where cross-team stories die.
